newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Critic, at 77, just keeps rockin' 'n' rollin'.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Critic, at 77, just keeps rockin' 'n' rollin'.

text.p: Jane Scott has trouble getting some of her friends to go to concerts with her.
The 77-year-old Scott is a rock 'n' roll writer for The Plain Dealer newspaper in Cleveland and few of her contemporaries care for the likes of Metallica or ZZTop.
"I don't have much success taking people my age with me," she said. "They've never heard of anything, you know? If I talk about Nirvana, my friends just get that blank look."
Younger friends have been more receptive.

"Jane took me to my first Grateful Dead concert," said librarian Cal Zunt, now 33 but a teenager at that time, who considers Scott a mentor and role model. "She's taught me that we're not bound by age definition and that any time of life can be interesting and dynamic," Zunt said.

Scott likes to say she was hired at the paper three days after disc jockey Alan Freed's legendary Moondog Coronation Ball in 1952. Freed is credited with popularising the term rock 'n' roll while working at Cleveland radio station WJW.

Editing the paper's teen section, writing a bit about music, Scott covered a 1966 Beatles news conference. "My first major interview was with John Lennon. Imagine," she said, song title plug not unintended.
She recalled Lennon as serious and gracious and Paul McCartney as flirtatious and talkative but "very genuine."
PAUL A FAN
Years later McCartney returned to Cleveland with Wings.

"He remembered me. He said I was the only middle-aged platinum blonde" in a herd of younger, mostly male reporters covering popular music. Scott, then in her 40s, said she was a bit motherly in appearance and McCartney "was very pleasant."

McCartney's publicist, New York-based Joe Dera, said he often chuckles when he sends novices on his staff to Cleveland gigs and they return to report that they have met Scott. "They tell me, 'She's as old as my grandmother, but she knows more about rock 'n' roll than I do,'" Dera said.

Scott, who has kept her distinctive blonde pageboy hairdo and quiet demeanor, is a local legend. As she made her way through a crowded blues club on a recent evening, a dozen people stopped her to chat, and at Cleveland's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum an "Evening with Jane Scott" slide show in January was standing room only.
"Jane is as important as any radio station that ever fostered careers," said Barry Gabel of Cleveland-based Belkin Productions, a regional concert promoter.
A Cleveland native, Scott has lived in the suburb of Lakewood most of her life. She has never married.
A junior high school classmate recalled her as the girl with the "Hit Parader" song list taped to the back of her Latin notebook.
Scott loved boogie-woogie as a girl and recalled the first record she owned was Count Basie performing "I Sent For You Yesterday and Here You Come Today."
She writes a weekly column and is one of the paper's two rock music writers. "I don't think about retiring," she said.
EARPLUGS WHEN NEEDED
Like former Cub Scout Jim Morrison, Scott likes to be prepared, saying, "I don't go anywhere without a camera, a sandwich and my earplugs."
She tries to hear as many performers as possible. "My theory is always to get there first."
Lou Reed, about whom she wrote in 1972 after the Velvet Underground broke up, said, "I love Jane Scott. I always have and I always will."

At the opening for the $92 million Rock Hall in 1995, many artists sought Scott out, museum communications director Tim Moore said. "Artists have great affection for her because of her years of commitment to music," he said. "She is a jewel."

Former music critic Michael Heaton, now a Plain Dealer columnist, said Scott publicised local garage bands as tirelessly as she covered groups like the Beatles, treating rock music seriously at a time most adults thought it a fad.
"Jane gave the music credibility by the amount of work she put in. She's been successful in two of the most chauvinistic fields in the world -- journalism and rock music," he said.

For a critic, Scott is not very critical, one co-worker said, adding, "Jane is so nice. She never says anything mean." But Moore had a different view. "She's not always enamoured of every performer but she loves so many different kinds of music that she writes about it with a very open mind," he said.

Scott said she dislikes "snooty little self-important people," admires Weird Al Yankovic for "taking the pomposity out of rock" and thinks the Beastie Boys are great people but wishes they'd stop using the "F" word.
"I have few regrets. One is that I didn't go to a show here with Elvis, Pat Boone and Bill Haley together," she said.

Scott likes that kind of diversity. Her career has juxtaposed Aretha Franklin, the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Tony Bennett and the Butthole Surfers, and she liked radio when in one hour a station might play Frank Sinatra, Bob Dylan, the Beach Boys and Jimi Hendrix.
"We shouldn't get stuck in any one category," she said. "Pop, rap, country, rock, it doesn't matter. It's all music."
